reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / KDIGO
clinicalPearls: Contrast-induced nephropathy is an acute, usually reversible decline in renal function occurring within a few days of intravascular iodinated contrast, once other causes have been excluded
The rise in creatinine typically begins within one to three days and peaks around three to five days, with recovery over one to two weeks in most cases
Pre-existing chronic kidney disease is the strongest risk factor, and the risk rises steeply when diabetic nephropathy is also present
Volume depletion, heart failure, higher contrast volumes, and concurrent nephrotoxins compound the risk
The most effective preventive measure is adequate intravenous volume expansion with isotonic fluid before and after contrast exposure
Non-essential nephrotoxic drugs should be withheld around the time of the study and the smallest necessary volume of contrast used
The true incidence of contrast-related injury after intravenous contrast in modern practice is lower than once believed, and the need for imaging should be weighed against a frequently modest risk
reference.pathophysiology: Contrast-induced nephropathy is thought to arise from a combination of renal medullary ischaemia and direct tubular toxicity. Iodinated contrast alters intrarenal haemodynamics, causing vasoconstriction and reduced medullary blood flow, which is particularly damaging to the metabolically active outer medulla. Contrast media also generate reactive oxygen species and exert direct toxic effects on tubular epithelial cells, and their osmotic and viscosity properties can impair tubular flow. The result is a predominantly acute tubular injury pattern. Patients with reduced baseline renal reserve, impaired autoregulation, or reduced effective circulating volume are least able to compensate for these insults, which explains the clustering of risk in chronic kidney disease, diabetes, and volume depletion.
additionalDifferentials: Ischaemic acute tubular necrosis from hypotension or the underlying illness
Atheroembolic (cholesterol embolisation) renal disease after arterial procedures
Progression of underlying chronic kidney disease
additionalInvestigations: Baseline and serial serum creatinine with estimated GFR before and after contrast exposure
Urinalysis and urine microscopy to help distinguish tubular injury from other causes
Assessment of volume status and review of the medication list for other nephrotoxins
Consideration of atheroembolic disease (eosinophilia, skin changes) after arterial catheterisation
Renal ultrasound if obstruction or another structural cause is suspected
redFlags: Progressive or non-recovering renal function suggesting an alternative or additional cause
Oliguria or features of established acute kidney injury requiring supportive care
Signs of atheroembolism such as livedo, digital ischaemia, and eosinophilia after arterial procedures
Hyperkalaemia, acidosis, or fluid overload indicating a need for closer monitoring or dialysis
reference.prognosis: Most episodes are mild and self-limiting, with renal function returning toward baseline within one to two weeks. However, an episode is associated with longer hospital stay, higher risk of needing dialysis in susceptible patients, and worse long-term cardiovascular and renal outcomes, so prevention in high-risk individuals remains important.
pitfalls: Withholding a clinically necessary contrast study out of exaggerated fear of nephropathy in a low-risk patient
Failing to provide adequate periprocedural volume expansion in high-risk patients
Attributing all post-contrast creatinine rises to contrast without considering atheroembolism or ischaemic injury
Overlooking continued exposure to other nephrotoxic drugs during the vulnerable period
management: Prevention is the cornerstone: peri-procedural intravenous volume expansion with isotonic crystalloid before and after iodinated contrast in at-risk patients
Use the smallest feasible volume of iso- or low-osmolar contrast and avoid closely spaced repeat contrast studies
Withhold non-essential nephrotoxins around exposure (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, diuretics) and hold metformin per local protocol
Once established, provide supportive care: maintain euvolaemia, avoid further nephrotoxic agents, and correct electrolyte and acid-base disturbances
Monitor serial serum creatinine, estimated GFR and urine output to track the expected early rise and recovery
Escalate to renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload or uraemic complications in severe acute kidney injury
Refer to nephrology for non-recovering or dialysis-requiring cases and risk-stratify high-risk patients (chronic kidney disease, diabetic nephropathy) for contrast-free alternative imaging
